sections.h: The Book of Baruch: Baruch in Babylon
sections.b: The deuterocanonical book that bears his name opens with Baruch in Babylon, reading his book aloud to the exiled King Jeconiah and the exiles "in the fifth year" after Jerusalem burned, then sending money and the temple's silver vessels to the priests in Jerusalem (Baruch 1:1–14). His family line matches Jeremiah 32:12. But Jeremiah's own book takes Baruch to Egypt with Jeremiah (Jeremiah 43:6), and a tradition kept by Jerome has him die there, which Gigot's Catholic Encyclopedia article admits "conflicts with" Baruch 1. Toy saw no reason to think Baruch was ever in Babylon. The book is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians and is placed among the Apocrypha by Protestants; whether Baruch wrote it is weighed on the book's opening pages.

Baruch 1–5 is written for a scattered people. Its frame shows exiles in Babylon praying for Nebuchadnezzar, as Jeremiah told them (Jeremiah 29:7), and sending a confession to be read in Jerusalem (Baruch 1:10–14). The confession explains the exile as the covenant's curse come true (Baruch 1:20; 2:2–5) and claims Moses' promise that in exile the people would come to their senses and be brought home (Baruch 2:29–35). The wisdom poem calls exile a living death among strangers (Baruch 3:10–11), and the closing poems picture mother Jerusalem's children gathered from east and west (Baruch 4:36–37; 5:5–6).

sections.h: Baruch: wisdom given to Israel as the law
sections.b: The poem of Baruch 3:9–4:4 asks Job 28's question: who has found where wisdom lives? Not rulers, merchants, the wise men of Teman or the giants of old; no one climbed into the sky for her or crossed the sea (Baruch 3:29–30, using Deuteronomy 30:12–13). Only the creator knows her, and he "gave it to his servant Jacob" (Baruch 3:37). Then she is named: "She is the book of the commands of God, the law that lasts forever" (Baruch 4:1), as Sirach 24:23 says. The verse between, "After this she was seen on earth and went about among human beings" (Baruch 3:38), was read by many early Christians of the incarnation; the Plain reads it of wisdom given as the law, and Toy called it a Christian addition.

uncommon: Crawford Toy judged Baruch 3:38 ("After this she was seen on earth") a Christian addition to a Jewish poem.

sections.h: The law as wisdom in Baruch
sections.b: Baruch 4:1 names the wisdom that no nation found: "She is the book of the commands of God, the law that lasts forever. Everyone who holds on to her is headed for life; those who let go of her will die." With Sirach 24:23 it is one of the earliest texts to identify personified Wisdom with the Torah. It builds on Moses' word that keeping the law "will show your wisdom and your understanding to the peoples" (Deuteronomy 4:6) and ends: "How happy we are, Israel! What pleases God has been made known to us" (Baruch 4:4).

sections.h: Who has climbed into the sky? Deuteronomy 30 in Baruch and Romans
sections.b: Moses said the commandment is "not in the sky" and "not on the far side of the sea" (Deuteronomy 30:12–13). Baruch asks the same of wisdom: "Who has climbed up into the sky and taken her, and brought her down from the clouds?" (Baruch 3:29), and answers that God brought her near as the law (Baruch 3:37–4:1). Paul quotes Deuteronomy, not Baruch, and applies the lines to Christ (Romans 10:6–8). The two texts show that Jews of the time read Deuteronomy 30 as being about the word or wisdom God brings down to people. Christians then read Baruch 3:38, wisdom "seen on earth", beside John 1:14.

sections.h: "This is our God": Baruch 3:36–38 in the early church
sections.b: Early Christians read Baruch 3:36–38 as a prophecy of Christ: "This is our God; no other will be reckoned next to him ... After this she was seen on earth and went about among human beings." Cyprian quoted it as from "Jeremiah" under the heading "That Christ is God"; the Apostolic Constitutions (5.20) quoted it as foretelling Christ; Hippolytus argued against Noetus, who used it to say the Father himself appeared on earth, that it speaks of the Son. The Orthodox Church reads Baruch 3:36–4:4 at Vespers on Christmas Eve. The Greek, read with Baruch 4:1, more naturally speaks of wisdom given as the law.

In Baruch 4:9–29 Jerusalem speaks as a widowed mother. She mourns to the towns around her that the Everlasting has taken her sons and daughters captive, and says goodbye to her children: "Walk on, children, walk on; I am left behind, alone" (Baruch 4:19), while promising that God will give them back "with joy and gladness for all time" (Baruch 4:23). From Baruch 4:30 the poet comforts her in Isaiah's words, dresses her in God's glory and gives her a new name, "Peace of Righteousness" and "Glory of Godliness" (Baruch 5:4).

sections.h: Baruch: the mother and her neighbors
sections.b: Baruch develops the city-as-woman picture of Lamentations: Jerusalem is the mother who "nursed" Israel while God "fed" them (Baruch 4:8), a widow "abandoned by many" (Baruch 4:12), and her neighbors, the towns around Zion, are pictured as women too (Baruch 4:9, 4:14, 4:24; the Greek is feminine). The enemy city is a woman also, glad at Jerusalem's fall and then left empty herself (Baruch 4:33).

Baruch 1:11–12 has the exiles pray for "Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon" and "his son Belshazzar", the same picture as Daniel 5, where Nebuchadnezzar is called his father. Babylonian records make Belshazzar the son of Nabonidus. Toy notes writers of his time who saw in the two princes a veiled reference to Vespasian and his son Titus, which would put the book after AD 70.

In Baruch 1:11–12 the exiles ask the priests in Jerusalem to pray for the life of Nebuchadnezzar, the king who burned the city, "so that they last on earth as long as the sky does", and they hope to live "in the shade" of the Babylonian kings and serve them. The request follows Jeremiah's letter (Jeremiah 29:7) and the prophet's call to serve the king of Babylon (Baruch 2:21; Jeremiah 27:11–12).

Baruch 1:3 makes the exiled King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) the first hearer of Baruch's book, read in Babylon with all the exiles "from the least to the greatest". Jehoiachin was indeed in Babylon from 597 BC until his release by Evil-merodach (2 Kings 25:27).

Baruch 1:15–3:8 is a long confession sent to be read in the temple on feast days (Baruch 1:14). Its first half follows Daniel's prayer phrase by phrase (Daniel 9:4–19): "Righteousness belongs to the Lord our God, but to us belongs the shame of our faces" (Baruch 1:15; Daniel 9:7). Toy judged that Baruch borrows from Daniel. It goes on into a plea built from Jeremiah and Deuteronomy, and it grounds its plea on God's compassion, not on "what our ancestors and our kings did right" (Baruch 2:19).

Baruch's confession reads Jerusalem's fall as Deuteronomy's curses come true: "the curse that the Lord laid on Moses his servant" (Baruch 1:20), parents eating their children "just as it is written in the law of Moses" (Baruch 2:2–3; Deuteronomy 28:53), Israel "underneath and not on top" (Baruch 2:5; Deuteronomy 28:13, 44), and a shameless nation with a foreign tongue (Baruch 4:15; Deuteronomy 28:49–50).

sections.b: Baruch ends with a new exodus from the east: God orders every high mountain brought low and the ravines filled "so that Israel may walk safely in the glory of God" (Baruch 5:7), the woods shade them (Baruch 5:8), and God leads them "by the light of his own glory" (Baruch 5:9). The pictures come from Isaiah 40:3–5 and run very close to Psalms of Solomon 11:2–7; Toy left open which text borrowed from the other.
sections.refs: Baruch 5:5–9; Isaiah 40:3–5; Isaiah 52:12; Psalms of Solomon 11:2–7; Luke 3:4–6

sections.h: Baruch: demons in the enemy city
sections.b: Baruch 4:35 says of the city that took Jerusalem's children: "Fire from the Everlasting will fall on her for many long days, and demons will make her their home." It stands between Isaiah's goat-demons in ruined Babylon (Isaiah 13:21, where the Greek has daimonia) and Revelation's cry that Babylon "has become a home for demons" (Revelation 18:2).

sections.h: "The Everlasting" and "the Holy One" in Baruch
sections.b: Baruch 4–5 uses two adjectives as names for God: ho aiōnios, "the Everlasting" (Baruch 4:10, 4:14, 4:20, 4:22, 4:24, 4:35; 5:2), and ho hagios, "the Holy One" (Baruch 4:22, 4:37; 5:5). In Baruch 4:22 they stand together: joy comes "from the Holy One" over the mercy coming "from the Everlasting, your Savior". Genesis 21:33 has "the LORD, the Everlasting God".
sections.refs: Baruch 4:10; Baruch 4:22; Baruch 5:2; Baruch 5:5; Genesis 21:33; Isaiah 40:28

sections.h: "The prayer of the dead of Israel" (Baruch 3:4)
sections.b: Baruch 3:4 asks God to hear "the prayer of the dead of Israel", a few verses after saying the dead in Hades cannot give God glory (Baruch 2:17). Bullard and Hatton's UBS handbook suggests the Greek translator misread a Hebrew word: metei can mean "the dead of" or "the men of" (the phrase "men of Israel" stands in Isaiah 41:14). Others read "dead" as exiles who are as good as dead (Baruch 3:10–11). The verse has also been cited in discussion of whether the dead pray for the living (see 2 Maccabees 15:12–14).
